content: The Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that the benefits of using upper limb veins for catheter insertion likely outweigh those of using lower limb veins in most clinical scenarios. They found no significant uncertainty or variability in the values associated with the outcomes of interest. The balance of effects appeared to favor upper limb vein use due to ease of insertion and reduced risk of complications. A review of the literature identified 25 non-randomized studies (NRSIs) comparing catheter insertion in the upper versus lower limbs in adults and neonates. Three studies included mixed populations, but no studies were identified for children or adolescents. Eight studies focused on peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs), while 17 focused on peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs). These studies collectively reported findings on 16,665 patients or catheters from various countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, and India. Seventeen NRSIs were rated as having some risk of bias, while eight were rated as having a high risk of bias. For PIVC insertion in adults, the evidence was highly uncertain regarding the effect of upper versus lower limb insertion on phlebitis or thrombophlebitis. Two studies reported phlebitis rates ranging from 6% to 42% in the upper limb and 9% to 72% in the lower limb. The largest study, involving 1,251 patients, showed little to no difference between groups when stratified by the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score. No studies reported on catheter-associated bloodstream infections (CABSI), bloodstream infection (BSI)-related mortality, sepsis, all-cause mortality, or complications related to catheter insertion. For PIVC insertion in children and adolescents, the evidence was very uncertain. One cohort study involving 455 patients reported no cases of CABSI or local infections in either the upper or lower limb groups. Complication rates ranged from 21% to 30% in the upper limb group and 29% to 100% in the lower limb group. No studies reported on BSI-related mortality, sepsis, all-cause mortality, or phlebitis/thrombophlebitis. For PIVC insertion in neonates, two cohort studies involving 643 patients suggested little to no difference in complications between upper and lower limb insertion. Complication rates ranged from 65% to 83% in the upper limb group and 65% to 79% in the lower limb group. Evidence was very uncertain regarding CABSI and local infections, with no cases reported in one study. No studies reported on BSI-related mortality, sepsis, all-cause mortality, or phlebitis/thrombophlebitis. For PICC insertion in neonates, the evidence was very uncertain. Five cohort studies involving 1,355 patients reported CABSI rates ranging from 5% to 10% in the upper limb group and 0% to 25% in the lower limb group. Sepsis rates ranged from 5% to 12% in the upper limb group and 2% to 23% in the lower limb group. Local infection rates ranged from 0% to 5% in the upper limb group and 0% to 43% in the lower limb group. All-cause mortality rates ranged from 5% to 6% in the upper limb group and 1% to 6% in the lower limb group. Phlebitis/thrombophlebitis rates ranged from 0% to 10% in the upper limb group and 0% to 21% in the lower limb group. Complication rates ranged from 3% to 40% in the upper limb group and 20% to 30% in the lower limb group. No studies reported on BSI-related mortality. The GDG considered that the resources required for PIVC insertion in the upper limb were negligible and that cost-effectiveness likely favored upper limb use due to ease of insertion. They also noted that lower limb PIVC insertion was associated with an increased risk of phlebitis and greater restriction of patient mobility, which could affect both patient and healthcare worker (HCW) acceptability. For PICC insertion in neonates, the GDG found that cost-effectiveness likely favored upper limb use, despite potential limitations in neonatal movement. The GDG suggested that if lower limb veins are used for PIVC insertion in emergencies, the catheter should be replaced with an upper limb catheter as soon as practicable to reduce infection risk. They also recommended the use of occlusive dressings for PIVCs and PICCs, provided they allow direct daily inspection of the insertion site for signs of infection. However, non-occlusive dressings may be preferred in cases of excessive exudate at the insertion site. The GDG emphasized the need for further research on optimal dressing types, the benefits and harms of chlorhexidine-containing dressings, and the development of cost-effective occlusive dressings suitable for all climates, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). They also highlighted the importance of ensuring that clinicians performing PIVC insertion are appropriately trained, regardless of whether they are part of a formal insertion team.
